big_idea: Fair-share with up to 20 items can use up to 10 sharers.
learning_intention: We are learning to share up to 20 items fairly between 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, or 10 friends and to write the result with a mixed number when needed.
student_learning_goal: I can share up to 20 items fairly between 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, or 10 friends and write the result with a mixed number when needed.
success_criteria: I can share 12, 15, 18, or 20 items fairly between any of 2-10 friends.
I can cut the leftover into the right fraction (matching the number of sharers).
I can write the per-friend share as a mixed number (e.g., 2 1/4).
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Sammy the Sharer — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Anchor chart 'Match the Fraction to the Sharers' (2→halves, 3→thirds, 4→fourths, 5→fifths, 6→sixths, 8→eighths, 10→tenths)
Lesson 4 fair-share tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Sammy has 18 paper treats. He needs to share fairly between 8 friends. How does he do it?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Sammy the Sharer puppet in hand. 'Friends — Sammy is having a party. He has 18 paper treats. 8 friends are coming. How does he share fairly?'

Place 8 paper plates on the floor. 'Watch Sammy deal.' Deal one treat per plate, going around: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 (one round, each plate has 1). Continue: 9-16 (two rounds, each plate has 2). 'How many left?' '2 left over.'

'2 leftover treats, 8 friends. Each friend should get an EQUAL share of the leftover. 8 friends share 2 treats fairly — each treat cut into 8 pieces? Wait, no — 2 treats divided 8 ways means each friend gets 2/8.'

Watch carefully. 'Each treat gets cut into 4 (eighths is too small to manage on paper). One treat = 4 fourths. 2 treats = 8 fourths. 8 fourths divided by 8 friends = 1 fourth each. So each friend gets a 1/4-treat extra. 2 + 1/4 each = 2 1/4.' Write 18 ÷ 8 = 2 1/4.

'2 1/4 is a MIXED NUMBER — 2 wholes plus 1/4 of another whole. We use mixed numbers when sharing doesn't come out even.'

Now show the rule. Write on the chart:
2 sharers → halves
3 sharers → thirds
4 sharers → fourths
5 sharers → fifths
6 sharers → sixths
8 sharers → eighths (or fourths, whichever fits)
10 sharers → tenths

'Match the FRACTION to the NUMBER of sharers. That's Sammy's rule.'

'Today we'll practice fair-sharing with lots of different counts and sharer numbers.'
student_actions: Watch Sammy deal 18 treats to 8 plates.
Help find the leftover after the rounds (2 left).

steps.instruction: Whole group: practice 4 more shares. (a) 12 ÷ 4 = 3 (even). (b) 15 ÷ 5 = 3 (even). (c) 20 ÷ 8 = 2 1/2 (each friend gets 2 wholes + half a leftover). (d) 16 ÷ 6 = 2 2/3 (the trickiest — 4 leftover for 6 friends = 2/3 each by cutting two leftovers into 3 each). For tricky cases, focus on the matching rule.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Four more shares. Apply Sammy's rule.' For (d), slow down: 'We have 4 leftovers for 6 friends. We can't cut into thirds because 4 isn't divisible by 3. But we can cut each leftover into 3 thirds, giving 12 thirds total. 12 thirds for 6 friends = 2 thirds each. So 2 + 2/3 = 2 2/3.'

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 minutes each). Station A: Even Shares — pair has 8 scenarios with whole-number quotients (12÷3, 12÷4, 15÷5, 16÷4, etc.). Station B: Mixed-Number Shares — pair has 6 scenarios with leftovers (18÷8, 14÷4, 17÷5, etc.). Station C: Sammy's Choice — pair receives a number of treats (16) and chooses how many friends to share with from 2-10. They write 3 different scenarios.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: child must find ALL ways 16 can be evenly shared (16 ÷ 1, 16 ÷ 2, 16 ÷ 4, 16 ÷ 8, 16 ÷ 16) — the factors of 16. Discuss why these specific numbers work.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs at Station C: '16 has FACTORS that divide evenly. What are they?' Lead to: '1, 2, 4, 8, 16'.

steps.instruction: Discuss the why. 'Why does the fraction match the number of sharers? Because dividing one whole into N equal pieces gives N pieces — and N pieces divided among N people = 1 each. Same logic when there are M leftover items to divide N ways.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Use the 18÷8 example: 'We had 2 leftover treats. 2 treats × 4 fourths each = 8 fourths. 8 fourths ÷ 8 friends = 1 fourth each. The fraction matches.'

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the fair-share tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Hand them a scenario and ask 'How will you share? What fraction?' Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Children stay at Station A (Even Shares) for both rotations. Use small dividends (12 ÷ 3, 12 ÷ 4) to anchor the pure equal-sharing concept.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch scenarios: 24 items, 7 sharers (24 ÷ 7 = 3 3/7). Discuss whether sevenths work. (Yes — but harder visually.)
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide the matching-rule reference card. Provide picture-supported scenarios.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Build with paper treats and physical plates. Movement learners can deal and cut.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: shares fairly with right number of equal groups; matches the fraction to the number of sharers; writes mixed numbers correctly.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the fair-share tracker per child.
tracker_columns: Shares fairly with right number of groups
Matches fraction to number of sharers

discussion_prompts: If 5 friends share, what fraction matches?
What's a mixed number? Why do we use them?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child writes one share they figured out today on a sticky note: '___ ÷ ___ = ___ each.' Notes go on the anchor chart on the way out.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Equal-sharing accuracy, matching-fraction-to-sharers rule application, and mixed-number writing across 3-5 scenarios per child.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 4 captures B1.6 mastery for Grade 3. Children who handle 18÷8 and 17÷5 with the right fractions are at L4.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child shares 18 cookies among 8 friends as 2 each plus a leftover but cannot match the right fraction — repairing the leftover-fraction calculation
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
The most common Grade-3 trap on B1.6 (fair-share with 2-10 sharers) is the leftover-fraction calculation. Children deal 18 ÷ 8 correctly to 2 each with 2 leftover. They know they need to split the leftovers — but they don't know HOW. They might cut the 2 leftovers in half (= 4 halves for 8 friends — only enough for half the group) or in thirds (= 6 thirds for 8 friends — uneven). The right move is to cut each leftover into 4 fourths (= 8 fourths for 8 friends = 1 fourth each).

The distinction matters because the leftover-fraction is what makes B1.6 conceptually distinct from Grade 2. Children who can fair-share without leftovers are at Grade 2 level; children who can match the leftover-fraction to the sharer count are at Grade 3 level. The expanded walkthrough covers the precise moment when a child has 2 leftover treats and 8 friends and freezes.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station B (Mixed-Number Shares). The card is 18 ÷ 8. The child has dealt 16 treats to 8 plates (2 each) and has 2 leftover treats. They look at the teacher.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Two leftover treats, 8 friends. Each friend should get a fair share of the leftover. How can we cut these 2 treats so 8 friends each get the same?'

Wait. The child often says 'cut in half' (2 treats × 2 halves = 4 halves; only 4 friends get a piece — not fair) or 'cut in fourths' (2 treats × 4 fourths = 8 fourths; 1 fourth each — fair!).

If they say halves: 'Halves give us 4 pieces for 8 friends. Some friends would get nothing. Not fair.' Lead them to fourths.

If they say fourths: 'Yes! Each treat into 4 fourths gives us 4 + 4 = 8 fourths. 8 fourths divided 8 ways = 1 fourth each. So each friend gets 2 + 1/4 = 2 1/4.'

Write the explicit calculation:
18 ÷ 8 = 2 with 2 leftover
2 leftover treats × 4 fourths each = 8 fourths
8 fourths ÷ 8 friends = 1 fourth each
Final: 2 1/4 each.

Now the rule. 'When you have leftovers, ask — how many EQUAL pieces do I need to divide them into? You need ENOUGH pieces for ALL the friends. So cut each leftover into pieces such that the total is at least equal to the number of friends.'

If the child STILL freezes: try a simpler scenario first. 14 ÷ 4 = 3 with 2 leftover. 'Cut each leftover into 2 halves = 4 halves total = 1 half each. 14 ÷ 4 = 3 1/2.' Build up from simpler cases.

Long-term recovery: include daily warm-ups with mixed-number shares for a week. Children build the matching-fraction reflex.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Knows there's a leftover but cannot match the right fraction. Most common at the start of Lesson 4.
(Mid) Cuts in halves first; recognises it's not enough; tries fourths with prompting.
(Strong) Auto-matches: '8 friends, 2 leftover — cut each into 4 fourths, 8 fourths ÷ 8 = 1/4 each.' Writes mixed number 2 1/4.
(Stretched) Volunteers an alternative: 'I could also call this 2 + 2/8 — same thing as 2 1/4.' Sees fraction equivalence.
common_misconceptions: All leftovers get cut in half. (Halves-default. Repair: match fraction to sharers.)
If sharers > leftovers, give one whole leftover to one friend. (Unfair. Repair: cut into pieces small enough that all friends get an equal share.)
Mixed numbers are weird. (Confusion about notation. Repair: 2 1/4 = 2 wholes + 1 fourth — show with paper treats.)
recovery_moves: Always count: 'How many pieces do I need? At least one per friend.' Anchors the cutting decision.
Build with paper treats. Visible cuts make the equivalence concrete.
Connect to the matching-rule chart. 8 friends → eighths (or fourths, since fourths × 2 = eighths).

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of B1.6 (fair-share with up to 10 sharers, 20 items).

parts_outline.task: Four even-share scenarios. Child draws the share and writes the per-plate count.
Four mixed-number scenarios (18÷8, 14÷4, 17÷5, 16÷6). Child draws, cuts the right fraction, writes the mixed number.
Open prompt: 'Sammy has 20 items. List 5 ways he could share them fairly with different friend counts (between 2 and 10).'
